extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent attorneys/applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent claims for definiteness, written-description/enabling support, and related formal issues under 35 U.S.C. 112 (and pre‑AIA equivalents), including treatment of Markush groups, functional/negative/omnibus/product-by-process/use claims, multiplicity, and means‑plus‑function limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving ambiguity of functional limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: During prosecution, applicant may resolve ambiguities of a functional limitation by: (1) using a quantitative metric (e.g., numeric limitation) rather than a qualitative functional feature; (2) demonstrating that the specification provides a formula for calculating a property along with examples that meet and do not meet the claim limitation; (3) demonstrating that the specification provides a general guideline and examples sufficient to teach a person skilled in the art when the claim limitation was satisfied; or (4) amending the claims to recite the particular structure that accomplishes the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are example remediation routes; examiners should consider these approaches when determining whether language is ambiguous. The primary inquiry is whether the language leaves room for ambiguity or whether the boundaries are clear and precise. Other relevant factors may vary by art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush group treatment (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting a list of alternatives (Markush claim) is an acceptable claim construction and should not necessarily be rejected as confusing under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Treatment is not governed by particular format (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C' or 'A, B, or C').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2117 and § 706.03(y) for additional guidance. Evaluate Markush groupings on their facts; the listing (Markush group) is a recognized drafting technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed vs open Markush groups (indefiniteness risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush grouping is a closed group of alternatives when selection is from a group 'consisting of' the recited alternatives. If a Markush grouping requires selection from an open list (e.g., 'comprising' or 'consisting essentially of'), the claim should generally be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite because it is unclear what other alternatives are intended to be encompassed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If combinations or mixtures are intended, include qualifying language (e.g., 'at least one member selected from the group' or 'or mixtures thereof'). Cite Abbott Labs. v. Baxter and MPEP § 2111.03 as relevant authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush breadth and indefiniteness (when excessive breadth causes rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush group may include many alternatives, and breadth alone is not indefiniteness; however, if the grouping is so expansive that persons skilled in the art cannot determine the metes and bounds of the claimed invention (e.g., massive number of distinct chemical alternatives that cannot be envisioned), the claim may be indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether skilled artisans can determine the scope; if not, a rejection for indefiniteness under 112(b) is appropriate. Breadth ≠ indefiniteness per se (In re Gardner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminishing scope and double inclusion in Markush groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of Markush claims of diminishing scope or double inclusion of an element by members of a Markush group is not, by itself, a sufficient basis for objection or rejection. The facts of each case must be evaluated to determine whether multiplicity or indefiniteness results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the practice renders claims indefinite or results in undue multiplicity. Redundancy (e.g., generic and specific terms both listed) does not automatically render a claim indefinite (Eli Lilly v. Teva example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'optionally' in alternative lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the term 'optionally' (e.g., 'containing A, B, and optionally C') has been held acceptable where there is no ambiguity as to which alternatives are covered. Where ambiguity arises because the list of potential alternatives can vary, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Cordova and Ex parte Wu support that 'optionally' can be acceptable; the key is absence of ambiguity in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative limitations (exclusionary provisos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative limitations or exclusionary provisos are not inherently ambiguous or uncertain; they comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) so long as the boundaries of the patent protection sought are set forth definitely. However, any negative limitation must have basis in the original disclosure; lack of basis may require rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older skepticism about negative limitations may be distinguished by facts; if alternative elements are positively recited in the specification, they may be excluded in the claims. Lack of literal basis for a negative limitation is not necessarily sufficient to establish lack of descriptive support—evaluate facts and precedent (In re Johnson, Ex parte Parks; MPEP § 2163.07(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Old combination is not a valid ground for rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not be rejected on the ground of 'old combination' following the 1952 Patent Act; claims are proper so long as they comply with 35 U.S.C.112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply the pre‑1952 'old combination' doctrine (Lincoln Engineering) as a separate rejection; instead analyze statutory requirements. See Radio Steel, In re Bernhart, and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation is not a statutory ground for rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should not be rejected on the ground of 'aggregation' as non‑statutory. If a claim omits essential matter or fails to interrelate essential elements as defined by the specification, see MPEP § 2172.01 for proper treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure rejections are tied to statutory grounds (101/102/103/112) rather than non‑statutory 'aggregation' theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolix claims (long recitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be rejected as prolix only when long recitations or unimportant details render the scope of the claimed invention indefinite and the metes and bounds cannot be determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject for prolixity only when the claim's long recitations make the subject matter indefinite; provide reasoning about how claim language clouds metes and bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity / undue multiplicity of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: More than one claim may be presented if claims differ substantially and are not unduly multiplied. Where applicant presents an unreasonable number of repetitious claims which confuse rather than clarify, an undue multiplicity rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the rule of reason; undue multiplicity rejections should be rare and applied judiciously. Examiner procedure: contact applicant by telephone to request selection of claims for examination (see MPEP § 408). If applicant refuses, make an undue multiplicity rejection in the next Office action, request selection, and proceed to examine selected claims; preserve applicant's right to appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double inclusion: fact‑specific evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: No per se rule that double inclusion is improper; whether multiple inclusion of an element gives rise to indefiniteness must be evaluated on the facts of each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reasonable claim construction (In re Kelly) and examine whether double inclusion leads to ambiguity (e.g., device claims that can read the same element twice may be indefinite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product‑by‑process claims are permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Product‑by‑process claims, which define the claimed product in terms of the process by which it is made, are proper so long as it is clear that the claim is directed to the product and not the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may present claims of varying scope using product‑by‑process language. Cite Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma and In re Luck for supporting precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims combining product and process in the same claim (improper)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single claim that claims both an apparatus and the method steps of using the apparatus is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b); such claims create confusion as to when infringement occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Katz (system claim with user actions) and IPXL Holdings v. Amazon. Avoid claims mixing statutory classes which create ambiguity about direct infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Use' claims and process claims lacking steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to claim a process without setting forth any steps generally raises an indefiniteness issue under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Such 'use' claims may also be improper under 35 U.S.C. 101; examiners should consider rejecting under alternative grounds (101 and 112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide based on authority and facts; sometimes recited steps like 'utilizing' have been held not indefinite (Ex parte Porter). If ambiguous, reject under both 101 and 112 to preserve grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omnibus claims are indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: An omnibus claim (e.g., 'A device substantially as shown and described') should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) because it fails to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.35 for such rejections. See MPEP § 706.03(d) and MPEP § 1302.04(b) for cancellation by examiner's amendment procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to figures or tables in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporation by reference to a specific figure or table in a claim is permitted only in exceptional circumstances where there is no practical way to define the invention in words; incorporation by reference is a 'necessity' doctrine, not for applicant convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer claims complete in themselves; reference characters corresponding to elements may be used in conjunction with recitation of same elements (see MPEP § 608.01(m)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical formula and structure claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to chemical compounds and compositions using chemical formulas should not be considered indefinite or speculative merely because a structure is not fully presented or because corroborating spectroscopic data is absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of corroborating data cannot be the basis for indefiniteness. Partial structures or claims by name/physical‑chemical characteristics or by making process are acceptable where a skilled artisan can identify the compound (see In re Fisher, Martin v. Johnson, Ex parte Brian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademarks or trade names in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of a trademark or trade name in a claim is not per se improper, but a trademark identifies a source, not the goods; using a mark as a limitation to identify or describe a material/product does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and renders the claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trademark appears and is not intended as a limitation, address why it is present. If it causes confusion as to claim scope, reject under 35 U.S.C.112(b). See MPEP § 608.01(v) for definitions and Ex parte Simpson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere function of a machine does not bar process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Process or method claims should not be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) solely because they define the inherent function of a disclosed machine or apparatus; an otherwise patentable process should not be rejected merely because the application discloses an apparatus which will inherently carry out the recited steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow In re Tarczy‑Hornoch: do not use inherent machine function alone as basis for indefiniteness rejection of process claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice compact prosecution (examine claims thoroughly early)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should review each claim for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review and identify all applicable grounds of rejection in the first Office action to avoid unnecessary delays (compact prosecution). When a term renders a claim indefinite, make a 112(b) rejection and also rejections over the prior art under 102/103 where applicable, stating how the indefinite term is being interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid piecemeal examination by rejecting each claim on all valid grounds available; when claiming indefiniteness, state on the record the interpretation applied with respect to prior art rejections (see 37 CFR 1.104(a)(1), In re Packard, and MPEP § 707.07(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art rejection when claim is indefinite (two approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is indefinite relative to prior art, two examination approaches are possible: (1) if uncertainty is limited and at least one interpretation renders the claim unpatentable, enter both (A) a 112(b) indefiniteness rejection and (B) a prior art rejection based on the interpretation that renders the prior art applicable (stating how the claim is being interpreted); (2) if there is great confusion as to proper interpretation, do not base a 103 rejection on substantial speculation about claim meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first approach is recommended to avoid piecemeal prosecution and to give applicant better appreciation of relevant prior art (see Ex parte Ionescu and In re Steele). Examiners must state how the claim is interpreted when making prior art rejections in these circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between 35 U.S.C.112(a) and (b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enabling) and 112(b) (definiteness) are separate and distinct. A specification disclosure not commensurate in scope with the claim does not by itself render the claim indefinite (112(b)) but indicates insufficient disclosure under 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification discloses a feature as critical or essential and the claims fail to recite it, a 112(a) rejection (lack of enabling/descriptive support) may be appropriate (In re Borkowski, In re Mayhew). Distinguish insufficiency of disclosure from indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments adding subject matter not described (new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is amended to include an invention that is not described in the application as filed, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre‑AIA first paragraph) as directed to subject matter not described in the specification may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate changes for written‑description support; see In re Simon and In re Panagrossi for examples where claims to a subcombination lacked description in the filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting 35 U.S.C.112(f) / pre‑AIA sixth paragraph (means‑plus‑function)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'means or step plus function' limitation should be interpreted under the broadest reasonable interpretation that is statutorily mandated in paragraph six; the PTO may not disregard the structure disclosed in the specification corresponding to such language when rendering a patentability determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the en banc In re Donaldson holding: identify corresponding structure/steps in the specification and limit the means‑plus‑function claim accordingly. These are guidelines consistent with binding precedent; they do not have the force of rulemaking.
